name: Portuguese Cistern
hero_subtitle: Vaulted underground hall with zenithal light — the jewel of the Portuguese City.

overview.title: El Jadida’s underground jewel
overview.p1: Built in the 16th century by the Portuguese, first as a warehouse or arsenal then converted into a cistern, this 34 × 34 m hall rests on 25 columns supporting Manueline vaults. A thin layer of water reflects the arches and the light falling through the central oculus.
overview.p2: The site served as a location for Orson Welles’ film Othello. The atmosphere is unique: silence, reflections and play of shadows. Visit preferably in the morning for natural light.
overview.p3: It is El Jadida’s most emblematic site and a must on any visit to the citadel.

food.li1: Fish restaurants at the port (5–10 min walk).
food.li3: Simple tables in the citadel streets.
food.li4: Do not eat inside the site (no facilities).
food.li5: Bring water before or after the visit.
food.p2: Cash remains useful for small places.

tips.title: Practical tips for the Portuguese Cistern

1.title: Opening hours
1.desc: Check the day’s hours; often closed on Tuesdays. Arrive early for the light.

2.title: Photos
2.desc: Damp floor: watch for reflections. Tripod useful if allowed.

3.title: Respect
3.desc: Do not touch the water or columns; stay in authorised areas.

q1.question: How long for the cistern?
q1.answer: 30 to 45 minutes is plenty for the visit and photos.

q2.question: Is there water on the floor?
q2.answer: Yes, a thin layer creates the famous reflections. Wear suitable shoes.

q3.question: Can I visit with children?
q3.answer: Yes, the site is accessible; watch the steps and damp floor.

q4.question: Is the cistern open every day?
q4.answer: Often closed on Tuesdays. Check local opening times before going.

q5.question: Do I need a guide?
q5.answer: Not mandatory, but a guide enriches the historical visit of the citadel.
